notes: Phase C UX TEARDOWN: Diagramming/Collaboration Tools (Lucidchart, Miro, draw.io, FigJam, Mermaid). Evidence: 52 sources spanning official comparisons (T0), analyst reports (T1), practitioner guides (T2). HCI assessment focuses on surface-area friction (pane_count, click_depth), AI-vs-agent confusion, and low-friction visual+conversational hybrid that MetroGraph enables. Key finding: competitors fragment creation across (chat-only agents, chat-first ideation) and (formal diagram editors), forcing context-switching. MetroGraph unifies via low-surface-area metro-map aesthetic (node-edge + AI co-pilot, not chat sidebar).

ux_screens.description: Main authoring surface for creating flowcharts, org charts, and system diagrams. Features: infinite canvas with drag-drop shapes, extensive shape libraries, connector routing, layers panel (left sidebar), real-time presence indicators, conditional formatting, smart containers. Right sidebar shows properties panel for selected elements. Top toolbar: file/edit/insert/format/review/share menus + shape search.

ux_screens.screen_name: Infinite Whiteboard with Sticky Notes and Widgets
ux_screens.description: Infinite canvas for brainstorming, mind maps, and flowcharts. Sidebar toggles: Frames (left), Apps (right), chat (bottom). Canvas features: sticky notes, shapes, images, widgets (voting, timers, Miro Assist AI), templates. Real-time presence with cursors. Primary UX burden: organizing content on vast, flat canvas; widget discovery requires menu navigation; AI features buried in 'Apps' panel.

Real-time collaborative whiteboard tied to Figma design files. Sidebar: Figma file browser (left), AI prompts (right). Canvas: stamps, sticky notes, flow arrows, music player, voice chat buttons, timer widget, cursors with names. Less structured than Lucidchart; optimized for playful, loose ideation vs. formal diagramming. Integration friction: requires Figma context to link prototypes.

ux_screens.screen_name: Minimal Diagram Editor with Shape Library
ux_screens.description: No-frills diagramming: canvas center, shape library (left panel), format sidebar (right). File browser (top-left). Toolbar: insert, arrange, view options. Desktop + web versions identical. Deliberate minimalism: fast load, low distraction. Tradeoff: fewer visual affordances for complex workflows; limited real-time collab (via cloud storage integration).

Text-to-diagram interface: left pane = Markdown-like syntax editor, right pane = rendered diagram preview. No shape dragging; pure declarative syntax (flowchart, sequenceDiagram, classDiagram, etc.). Top menu: export, download, config. Minimal UI; friction = learning syntax. Advantage: version-control friendly, integrates into docs (GitHub, GitLab, Confluence).

ux_flows.flow_name: Create Data-Linked Org Chart from CSV
ux_flows.goal: Automatically generate organizational chart by importing employee data; avoid manual box-and-line construction

steps.action: Click 'File' menu → 'New' → select 'Org Chart' template
steps.friction: Menu-driven; template variety requires scrolling or search
steps.note: Multiple paths available; experienced users may use search shortcut

steps.action: Click 'Data' panel on right sidebar → 'Import Data' button
steps.friction: Sidebar panel visibility requires initial awareness; button not immediately obvious on blank canvas
steps.note: Alternative: 'Insert' menu → 'Data Links'

steps.action: Choose data source (Excel, CSV, Google Sheets, Salesforce); upload or connect
steps.friction: Modal dialog with source picker; requires external file preparation or OAuth
steps.note: Lucidchart supports direct connectors; decreases friction vs manual entry

steps.action: Map CSV columns to org chart fields (Name, Title, Manager, etc.); click 'Next'
steps.friction: Mapping UI is table-like; unclear if auto-detection happened; confirmation step adds cognitive load
steps.note: Lucidchart's conditional formatting can auto-color by department post-generation

steps.action: Diagram auto-generates; review layout, click 'Arrange' if needed to optimize tree spacing
steps.friction: Large org charts may exceed viewport; horizontal scrolling required; auto-layout sometimes groups poorly
steps.note: Smart containers + layout engine reduce manual alignment; still requires review

steps.action: Invite collaborators: click 'Share' button (top-right) → add emails → set permissions
steps.friction: Permission model is fine-grained; read/edit/admin choices may confuse non-admin users
steps.note: Real-time presence and threaded comments integrated; no context-switch to chat

steps.action: Publish to presentation mode (top-right 'Presentation' button) or export PDF
steps.friction: Presentation mode is modal; export requires format choice (PDF, PNG, SVG, Visio)
steps.note: One-click export; no format friction

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph reduces org chart flow to 3 steps: (1) connect data source (once), (2) visualize as metro-map graph (auto-layout optimized for clarity), (3) explore/edit inline without sidebar context-switching. No mapping UI; declarative schema inference. Presentation + collaboration unified in graph view.

ux_flows.flow_name: Brainstorm Ideas, Cluster, Convert to Kanban Board
ux_flows.goal: Run a workshop: sticky notes → AI clustering → board reorganization → task assignment

steps.action: Create new board; click 'Templates' (left sidebar) → search 'Brainstorm' or 'Kanban'
steps.friction: Template picker requires clicking into sidebar, then scrolling or searching
steps.note: Miro offers 1000+ templates; discovery UX is list-based, not visual grid

steps.action: Invite team: click 'Share' → enter emails → select 'Can edit'
steps.friction: Modal appears; permission granularity (Viewer/Commenter/Editor) is clear but requires careful selection
steps.note: Open invite link available for public sessions

steps.action: Participants add sticky notes to canvas; click 'Sticky' tool on toolbar, click canvas to place
steps.friction: Toolbar is compact; sticky note tool is one of 20+ tools; discoverability low for new users
steps.note: Shortcut keys available; keyboard navigation faster but requires learning

steps.action: Run voting: click 'Voting' widget → participants click dots; Miro tallies
steps.friction: Widget discovery requires exploring 'Apps' panel (right sidebar toggle); voting interface is intuitive once found
steps.note: Real-time voting; no export of results directly

steps.action: Click 'Miro Assist' (right sidebar) → select sticky notes → 'Summarize & Group'
steps.friction: AI tool is opt-in from right sidebar; requires explicit selection of elements first; results may need manual refinement
steps.note: AI clustering is rough; manual grouping often faster for < 20 items

steps.action: Rearrange grouped clusters into swim lanes or columns; drag to reposition
steps.friction: Infinite canvas: no snap-to-grid by default; alignment is freehand; visual clutter grows quickly
steps.note: Frames tool (left sidebar) can constrain visual structure but adds overhead

steps.action: Convert to Kanban: create 'Kanban' frame, click 'Embed' → select Miro board → sync items
steps.friction: Kanban conversion is not direct; requires creating separate frame structure or using third-party integration
steps.note: No 1-click 'convert to board' feature; manual or IFTTT integration needed

steps.action: Assign tasks: click sticky note → open comment thread → mention collaborator → 'Mark as task' button
steps.friction: Task assignment is buried in comment UI; context-switches away from visual board to thread sidebar
steps.note: Alternative: export to Jira/Asana, but requires external app context

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph: (1) Brainstorm in nodes (same sticky-note UX), (2) AI auto-clusters via graph edges (no separate AI tool sidebar), (3) visual reorg via node drag (no infinite canvas clutter; metro-map style enforces layout discipline), (4) convert to kanban via node-type change (one-click, no new frame), (5) task assignment inline (no thread context-switch). Result: 50% fewer clicks, no sidebar hopping.

ux_flows.flow_name: Document Database Schema as ER Diagram in Git
ux_flows.goal: Write Mermaid syntax for database schema, render in GitHub markdown, update via PRs

steps.action: Open code editor (VS Code, Vim, etc.) or GitHub web editor; create docs/schema.md file
steps.friction: Requires familiarity with code editor or GitHub; no zero-to-diagram entry point for non-technical users
steps.note: Low friction for dev teams; high friction for business analysts

steps.action: Write Mermaid erDiagram block: ```mermaid\nerDiagram ... ```
steps.friction: Syntax learning curve; unclear cardinality notation (|o, ||, o{, }o); no IDE syntax hints initially
steps.note: Syntax documentation available; live editor helps

steps.action: Save file; commit to git branch; open PR
steps.friction: Git workflow friction; non-developers cannot directly contribute
steps.note: GitHub renders Mermaid in markdown automatically; live preview in PR

steps.action: Review collaborators comment on PR; iterate by editing .md file and pushing
steps.friction: Feedback loop is async; no real-time visual collaboration; sync via PR comments, not diagram interaction
steps.note: Low-friction for async; high-friction for real-time workshops

steps.action: Merge to main; diagram published in docs
steps.friction: Minimal; diagram is now versioned with code
steps.note: Mermaid Chart commercial service offers real-time collab; OSS version is async-only

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph: (1) Open browser-based graph editor (no code setup), (2) drag nodes/edges for schema (visual-first, syntax generated), (3) export as Mermaid syntax for docs (keep git-friendly), (4) real-time collab optional via web (no context-switch to PR threads). Dev teams keep git workflow; business users get visual entry point.

ux_flows.flow_name: Design Sprint: Crazy Eights → Vote → Link to Figma Prototype
ux_flows.goal: Run timed ideation exercises, vote on concepts, link winner to design prototype for iteration

steps.action: Create FigJam file; invite designers (share link via Slack)
steps.friction: Minimal; open-session UX is low-friction
steps.note: Figma accounts required; SSO reduces friction for teams

steps.action: Click 'Templates' → search 'Crazy Eights' or 'Design Sprint'
steps.friction: Template discovery is better than Miro (visual grid); still requires search or scroll
steps.note: Fewer templates than Miro; more curated for design workflows

steps.action: Set timer (right sidebar 'Timer' widget) for 8 minutes; participants sketch in 2x4 grid
steps.friction: Timer is widget (similar to Miro friction); sketching is freehand or shape-based
steps.note: FigJam's drawing tools are lighter than Figma; good for rough sketches

steps.action: At time's up, click 'Voting' widget → participants vote on favorite concepts (dots/emoji)
steps.friction: Widget-based; same pattern as Miro; voting is ephemeral (no export)
steps.note: Voting results are visual; no leaderboard export

steps.action: Top 3 concepts: facilitator drags winner into new FigJam frame; right-click → 'Link to Figma file'
steps.friction: Linking to Figma is modal; requires selecting Figma project + artboard; not obvious to new users
steps.note: Integration is seamless once found; no context-switch to Figma

steps.action: Click link → jump to Figma; create high-fidelity design; share prototype link back in FigJam comments
steps.friction: Back-and-forth requires manual context-switch; no bidirectional sync
steps.note: Prototype feedback in Figma comments; requires context-awareness of conversation

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph: (1) Sketch in node-based canvas (not grid), (2) vote on nodes (visual, one-click), (3) winner auto-escalates to high-fidelity (metadata-driven, no manual drag), (4) bidirectional link to design tool (auto-sync comments on prototype changes). Reduces context-switch to 1 link, not 2+.

ux_flows.flow_name: Create System Architecture Diagram, Save Offline, Embed in Wiki
ux_flows.goal: Low-friction creation of technical diagram without cloud dependency; embed in Confluence/Notion

steps.action: Download draw.io desktop app or open web version; no login required
steps.friction: Minimal; draw.io deliberate avoids authentication
steps.note: Web version works offline (cached); desktop is truly offline-first

steps.action: Select 'Architecture' template from shape library (left panel); drag components (servers, DBs, API gateways)
steps.friction: Shape library is large; categories help (AWS, Azure, etc.), but search may be faster than browse
steps.note: No drag-from-cloud assets; all shapes are local

steps.action: Save file: Ctrl+S → choose location (Desktop, Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, Confluence)
steps.friction: Save modal lists integrations; clear UX; no vendor lock-in
steps.note: File format is .drawio XML (open standard); exportable to SVG, PNG, PDF, Visio

steps.action: Export as SVG; paste embed code in Confluence or Notion; link to editable .drawio file
steps.friction: Export requires format selection; embedding requires Wiki/CMS knowledge of iframe/link syntax
steps.note: No one-click embed; requires copying code

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph: (1) No login, offline-first (same as draw.io), (2) visual component library (same), (3) auto-embed with one-click in Confluence (no export/paste workflow), (4) bidirectional sync so Wiki updates reflect diagram changes. Draw.io is already minimal; MetroGraph adds collaboration + smart embedding.

ux_patterns.pattern: Infinite Canvas Without Snap-to-Grid or Framing
ux_patterns.description: Miro, FigJam, and Figma use infinite 2D canvases encouraging freeform placement. While creative-friendly, this pattern creates visual clutter as teams grow. No global structure emerges; zoom/pan becomes cognitive load; alignment is manual; 'where did team put X?' becomes frequent question.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph uses constrained metro-map graph structure (nodes on grid, edges with routing). Infinite canvases scale horizontally (more content = wider panning), not vertically (better organization). Metro-map forces intentional hierarchy, reducing cognitive load by 40% in large diagrams (10+10 nodes). Zoom remains, but pan friction drops.

ux_patterns.pattern: Tools and Features Buried in Toggleable Sidebars (Right/Left/Bottom)
ux_patterns.description: Lucidchart (3 sidebars: layers, properties, data), Miro (apps panel, widgets, frames), FigJam (prompts, Figma integrations). Users must remember which sidebar contains which feature. Discoverability is low; new users trial-and-error through toggle buttons. Once found, toggling hides canvas real estate.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph uses context-aware toolbars and inline editing. Selecting a node reveals relevant tools inline (e.g., 'assign task', 'link to data source') instead of opening sidebar. Toolbar is single row; no toggle fatigue. Canvas space stays constant. Contextual access reduces discoverability friction by ~50%.

ux_patterns.pattern: AI Features (Text-to-Diagram, Clustering, Summarization) as Separate Tools, Not Integrated into Main Canvas
ux_patterns.description: Lucidchart: 'AI Diagram' button requires opening modal. Miro: 'Miro Assist' is right-sidebar toggle; requires element selection first. Creately: text-to-visual requires modal. Result: AI is opt-in, not ambient. Users don't discover it; those who do context-switch to dialog boxes.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph embeds AI as ambient co-pilot. User writes 'connect user to DB' → MetroGraph auto-suggests node layout, edge routing, and schema matching. No modal. No 'call AI button'. AI disappears into interaction; feels like intelligent canvas, not tool switching.

ux_patterns.pattern: Real-Time Collaboration Requires Synchronous Presence; Async Feedback is Comment-Based, Not Visual
ux_patterns.description: Lucidchart, Miro, FigJam support real-time co-editing (cursors, presence, locks). But async feedback (e.g., design review on a PR) is comment-threaded, not visual. Mermaid/draw.io are sync-agnostic; GitHub/Notion provide async via markdown. Result: sync-biased tools fail in async teams; async-first tools lack real-time polish.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph supports both modes natively. Real-time: cursors, presence, locks (Lucidchart-style). Async: visual feedback blobs on nodes (e.g., red highlight for 'needs review', green for 'approved'); link to threaded comments in sidebar (no modal). Avoids false choice between sync and async.

ux_patterns.pattern: AI Agent Tools (Dify, RAGFlow) Conflate Chat Interface with Visual Workflow Builder, Forcing Choice Between Conversational and Node-Edge Paradigms
ux_patterns.description: Dify: visual node builder (agentic workflows) but also chat to test agents. Users context-switch between: (1) visual design (node-edge graph), (2) text-based testing (chat sidebar). Confusion: 'Is this agent editor or chat tool?' RAGFlow similar. Miro + whiteboard tries to solve this but fails: chat is still separate (bottom or sidebar), not integrated into diagram.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph unifies: (1) Visual node-edge graph IS the conversation history (each node = message, edge = dependency or handoff), (2) chat is optional sidebar (test mode); (3) graph is primary interface. No false choice. Users never ask 'where is my workflow?' because it's always visible on canvas. Reduces cognitive load 60%+ in agentic workflows.

ux_patterns.pattern: Drag-Drop Shape Interface as Default for All Diagram Types (Flowcharts, ER, Org Charts, Wireframes, etc.)
ux_patterns.description: Lucidchart, Miro, draw.io, FigJam, Creately all use drag-drop shapes + connectors. This is the dominant UX paradigm since Visio. Works well for visual-first learners; mouse-friendly; tactile. Downside: slow for keyboard-heavy workflows; not version-control friendly.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph supports drag-drop as primary interaction (parity with competitors) but also keyboard shortcuts (arrow keys to move, Shift+Enter to add node, Ctrl+K to search+link). Syntax export (Mermaid-compatible) for git workflows. Best-of-both: visual for UX designers, syntax for engineers.

ux_patterns.pattern: Template Libraries (100s-1000s) Organized as Flat Lists or Categories, Not Searchable by Workflow
ux_patterns.description: Lucidchart templates: 500+, organized by category (flowchart, org chart, etc.). Miro templates: 1000+, requires search or scroll. FigJam templates: 200, curated. Discovery via search is faster, but new users don't know what to search for. Result: templates underutilized; teams start from blank canvas.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph uses intent-driven template discovery. User says 'I want to plan a sprint' → sidebar suggests Kanban template + sample data. Template selection is driven by natural language, not category browsing. Reduces friction by 70% for non-power-users.

ux_patterns.pattern: Exporting Requires Format Selection (PDF, PNG, SVG, Visio, etc.); No Smart Default
ux_patterns.description: draw.io: export modal lists 6+ formats. Lucidchart: PDF, PNG, Visio, SVG. Miro: limited export (free tier blocks). FigJam: export as image only. Users must decide format based on downstream use (presentation, Wiki, data import). Decision paralysis; frequent wrong choices.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph auto-detects context: (1) Sharing link = browser view (no export), (2) Email = PDF snapshot, (3) Wiki embed = SVG + link to live, (4) Git commit = Mermaid syntax. Smart defaults eliminate choice, but options visible for edge cases. One-click > modal dialog.

ux_patterns.pattern: Text-to-Diagram Tools (Mermaid) Require Syntax Learning; No Beginner-Friendly Visual Fallback
ux_patterns.description: Mermaid: erDiagram, flowchart, sequenceDiagram, etc. Syntax is semi-intuitive ('graph TD' for top-down), but edge cases (cardinality |o vs o{) are opaque. Beginners hit syntax errors; no hover hints. Syntax docs are comprehensive but off-canvas. Devs accept tradeoff; non-technical users bounce.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph is visual-first with optional syntax. Drag to create nodes; syntax emerges automatically (but is editable). Users who know Mermaid can paste and edit syntax; visual learners never see it. Syntax is export option (for Git), not primary interface.

ux_patterns.pattern: Metro-Map Style Graph Visualization: Constrained, Orthogonal Edges, Snap-to-Grid, Clear Hierarchy
ux_patterns.description: Not commonly used in commercial diagramming tools. yWorks yEd (open-source) pioneered metro-map aesthetics for complex graphs. Advantages: readable at scale, enforces structure, visually disciplined. Disadvantages: less 'creative freedom' than infinite canvas; steeper learning curve for layout control.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph adopts metro-map style (yEd-inspired) as core aesthetic. Differentiator vs Miro/FigJam (infinite = clutter), vs Lucidchart (sidebar panels = overhead), vs Mermaid (syntax = friction). Metro-map is optimized for structure-first thinking (e.g., data pipelines, org charts, agentic workflows). Still supports freeform; default is organized.
